title: Japan-Korea: Working Together as Like-Minded Countries?
gist: An examination of whether Japan and South Korea are genuinely 'like-minded' (dōshikoku), arguing the label is analytically empty unless alignment is tested issue by issue rather than inferred from shared democracy or shared US alliance status.

insights.claim: The term 'like-minded countries' has no settled definition in international politics and generally refers only to states sharing objectives or an understanding on specific issues, not to states sharing a regime type.
insights.speaker: ISOZAKI Atsuhito
insights.so_what: Treat 'like-minded' language in Indo-Pacific communiques as a rhetorical wrapper, not evidence of durable policy convergence.
insights.quote: There is no settled definition in international politics of “like-minded countries”
insights.locator: There is no settled definition in international politics

insights.claim: The concept of dōshikoku has become increasingly prominent in Japanese diplomatic discourse, signalling a deliberate framing device in Tokyo's foreign policy vocabulary.
insights.speaker: ISOZAKI Atsuhito
insights.so_what: Watch for dōshikoku framing as a tell for where Tokyo is trying to build coalitions without formal treaty commitments.
insights.locator: a concept increasingly prominent in Japanese diplomatic discourse

insights.claim: Japan and South Korea are not automatically like-minded because both are democracies, nor do their policies automatically align across diverse fields because both are US allies; the degree of alignment must be assessed issue by issue.
insights.speaker: ISOZAKI Atsuhito
insights.so_what: Discount assumptions of a coherent Japan-ROK bloc when modelling trilateral defense, export-control or supply-chain coordination; alignment is issue-specific and reversible.
insights.quote: The two countries are not automatically like-minded simply because they are both democracies
insights.locator: The two countries are not automatically like-minded

insights.claim: The frequently made argument that Japan and South Korea share values and should therefore strengthen cooperation on North Korea is the specific claim being challenged, implying North Korea policy is where the 'like-minded' assumption is weakest.
insights.speaker: ISOZAKI Atsuhito
insights.so_what: Expect friction rather than automatic convergence in Tokyo-Seoul North Korea policy, a recurring source of headline risk for trilateral initiatives.

insights.claim: Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae and South Korean President Lee Jae-myung held a summit meeting in Andong, South Korea on May 19, 2026, giving the bilateral relationship an active leader-level channel.
insights.speaker: ISOZAKI Atsuhito
insights.so_what: Leader-level engagement is intact, so any deterioration would be policy-driven rather than a breakdown in channels.
insights.locator: Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae and South Korean President Lee Jae-myung attend a summit meeting
